title: Lipid Profile & Electrolyte Analysis

references.label: Standard clinical chemistry laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Tietz Fundamentals of Clinical Chemistry)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: The lipid profile characterizes circulating lipid/lipoprotein fractions relevant to cardiovascular risk assessment, while electrolyte analysis measures the major ions that maintain fluid balance, acid-base status, and neuromuscular/cardiac function.
explanation: A standard lipid profile reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and either directly measured or (more commonly) calculated LDL cholesterol; because standard LDL calculation methods use triglyceride level as part of the formula, markedly elevated triglycerides can make a calculated LDL unreliable, requiring a direct LDL measurement or patient fasting-status review — a good example of why lipemia (already covered generically) specifically matters for this panel. Electrolyte panels (commonly sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate/CO2) are frequently measured by ion-selective electrode technology on the same automated chemistry analyzer used for the rest of the chemistry menu, and are especially sensitive to hemolysis (which releases intracellular potassium) — directly connecting to the laboratory's existing HIL-index concept.

comparison.left: Total cholesterol, HDL, triglycerides, LDL (measured or calculated)

comparison.right: Used for fluid/acid-base/cardiac status; highly hemolysis-sensitive (potassium)

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a calculated LDL is always as reliable as a directly measured one — the common calculation methods are affected by markedly elevated triglycerides.
